lead: The most international dish of Valencian gastronomy. Our contribution to world cuisine. Born in the Albufera in the 18th century, today it is Valencia’s gastronomic symbol to the world.

In Valencia, a good paella is not improvised: it is a ceremony. The wood fire — preferably orange or carob wood — the perfect level of the pan, the slow sofrito, the exact amount of water, the natural saffron and the patience not to stir the rice. Every step has its reason. The result, if all goes well, is a dry, loose and tasty rice with the legendary socarrat at the bottom — that golden, slightly toasted layer that is the signature of the good paella cook and that Valencians fondly fight over.

To find authentic paella, the non-profit Wikipaella initiative compiles restaurants that respect the original recipe. You can also consult the rice restaurants section of visitvalencia.com. Choose your setting: facing the Mediterranean in the Cabanyal? In the historic centre? In El Palmar beside the Albufera? Every place has its magic.

items.title: Paella Valenciana
items.subtitle: The original · Chicken, rabbit and huerta vegetables
items.body: The mother of all paellas. It was born in the villages of l’Albufera and l’Horta, where peasants cooked outdoors with whatever they had to hand: rice grown beside the lake, farmyard chicken and rabbit, bajoqueta (flat green bean), garrofó (large flat white bean), grated natural tomato, olive oil, saffron and salt. All cooked in a paella — the iron pan with two handles, with a wide base and shallow depth — over a wood fire. This dish of humble origin, born of the ingenuity of Valencian farmers, has become the most international dish of Spanish gastronomy. In 2022 the Universidad Católica de Valencia published a scientific study accrediting the ten authentic ingredients. No chorizo. No onion. No peas.

items.title: Seafood Paella
items.subtitle: The Mediterranean in a pan · Prawns, mussels, squid
items.body: The second great Valencian paella, born of the coast’s historic relationship with the sea. It dispenses with meat and replaces the water with a fish or seafood fumet that concentrates the flavour of the Mediterranean in every grain of rice. The ingredients vary according to the season and the market, but the result is always a rice of intense colour — with saffron and the seafood broth as the stars — that the Cabanyal, the Malvarrosa and the Port of Valencia embroider like no one else. Clóchinas (Valencian mussels), red prawn, cuttlefish and squid are the most common protagonists. Eating it facing the sea, with the Mediterranean breeze, is one of the most complete gastronomic experiences in the city.

items.title: Arroz del Senyoret
items.subtitle: Seafood already peeled · The most comfortable to eat · The young gentleman’s rice
items.body: The “arroz del señorito” — senyoret in Valencian — is the version of seafood paella in which all the seafood is served already peeled and cleaned, with no shells or labour. Its name ironically alludes to someone who did not want to get their fingers dirty while eating. Eating without working. The result is a rice just as tasty as seafood paella but more comfortable for the diner: every forkful directly combines the grain of rice with a piece of already-cleaned prawn or squid. It is common in restaurants in the El Carmen neighbourhood, the historic centre and the CAC area, and it is one of the rices most ordered by visitors who want the flavour of paella without the fuss.

items.title: Arroz a Banda
items.subtitle: Rice on the side · Seafaring origin · DO Arroz de Valencia
items.body: Arroz a banda — “on the side” in Valencian — is one of the Valencian rices most prized by chefs and gourmets. Its name explains its origin: on fishing boats, the sailors cooked the fish of the day with water, potato and onion to make the broth. With that broth — concentrated, marine, intense — they cooked the rice separately in the paella pan. This is how two dishes were born: the boiled fish (eaten first, “a banda”) and the rice (eaten afterwards). Today the rice is served on its own, with alioli and sometimes also the fish. It is a dry, golden-coloured rice with a deep flavour of the sea that has no equal. The restaurants of the Cabanyal and El Palmar de la Albufera make it with special mastery.

items.title: Wood fire
items.body: A wood fire — preferably orange wood — gives the socarrat and the authentic aroma

items.title: Level paella pan
items.body: The pan must be perfectly level so the rice cooks evenly

items.title: Don’t stir the rice
items.body: Once the rice is added, it is never stirred: the grain must absorb the broth on its own

items.title: The socarrat
items.body: The golden layer at the bottom — the socarrat — is the signature of the good paella cook. It is the reward

items.title: 5 min rest
items.body: After turning off the heat, rest for 5 minutes covered with a cloth before serving

items.title: Eat from the pan
items.body: Valencian tradition: the paella is placed in the centre and everyone eats directly from it

blocks.title: What you should know before ordering paella in Valencia
items: Authentic Valencian paella has chicken, rabbit, bajoqueta, garrofó and natural saffron — if it has chorizo or peas, it is not Valencian
The vessel is called “paella”, not “paellera” — in Valencian it means frying pan
Paella is always eaten at midday — Valencians do not eat paella for dinner; it is a Sunday and family dish
The socarrat — the toasted rice at the bottom — is the most prized part; ask for it if you like it and the restaurant masters it
Check Wikipaella (wikipaella.org) to find restaurants that guarantee the authentic recipe
In El Palmar beside the Albufera, paella and arroz a banda are especially authentic — it is the cradle of the dish
